question.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $6,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{6t}\,\,$ $1+t$ $t$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(6t)={e}^{6t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{6t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
6t{e}^{6t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}(1-6t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-{e}^{6t}t \\  & ={e}^{6t}(-t), \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{6t}t+{e}^{6t}(1-6t) \\  & ={e}^{6t}(1-t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}1+t & t \\ -t & 1-t\end{aligned}].
$$
